title: After Plummeting 62% This Year, Could Buying Intel Stock Today Set You Up for Life?
detail:
After Plummeting 62% This Year, Could Buying Intel Stock Today Set You Up for Life?
Will Healy, The Motley Fool

INTC
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Few stocks in the semiconductor sector have experienced a more dramatic fall this year than Intel (NASDAQ:INTC). Since reaching a peak closing price of nearly $141 per share in June, the stock has lost 62% of its value.

This has attracted bargain hunters who perceived Intel as a stock to own, and some may wonder whether Intel can set investors for life. Although Intel could beat the market over time, investors should not assume that a modest investment in the stock will bring financial independence. Here's why.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.

The reemergence of Intel

The prospect for Intel's return to prominence has dramatically improved under Lip-Bu Tan. The former Cadence Design Systems CEO has begun leveraging Intel's existing competitive advantages to compete in today's semiconductor industry.

In short, Tan is forging ahead where the previous Intel CEO, Pat Gelsinger, fell short. Intel has finally succeeded with its longtime plan to master advanced chip production with its 18A manufacturing process node.

This has allowed it to produce chips smaller than 2nm in the U.S., making it more competitive with the industry's dominant manufacturer, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSMC). That move could signal a revival in U.S. chip manufacturing.

Moreover, Fortune Business Insights forecasts that the artificial intelligence (AI) chip market will grow at a 30% compound annual rate through 2034, positioning Intel in a lucrative growth market.

Additionally, during Gelsinger's tenure, Intel opened its production capacity to third-party manufacturers. The foundry continues to flourish, attracting business from companies like Microsoft and Amazon's AWS. It has also made a deal with Tesla, with its upcoming 14A process node slated for production beginning in the second half of 2027.

Intel's growth prospects

Although these improvements could make Intel a market-beating stock, the law of large numbers hampers Intel's ability to make small investors wealthy.

When investors read stories about $5,000 investments turning into millions, that is usually a case of a small- or mid-cap stock eventually becoming one of America's largest companies.

Unfortunately for investors who want Intel to set them up for life, Intel remained in large-cap territory even at the height of its more recent troubles.

Key Takeaways

Avala Global, which manages $3.8 billion, opened stakes in Microsoft and Sandisk and raised its Intel stake 431% in the third quarter, its latest 13F shows.

Intel and Sandisk have each lost more than half their value since Sept. 30, while Microsoft is down 6%.

Analysts still see big upside in all three, though they've cut their Intel targets hard since early October.

Microsoft is the one the numbers back best, with rising estimates and a multiple below its long-run averages.

Avala Global isn't a household name. But last quarter, it made big bets on three of tech's most debated stocks.

Avala's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 16, shows a new stake in Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ), a 431% bigger position in Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) and a new stake in Sandisk (SNDK:NASDAQ). The firm manages $3.8 billion in all, and its 13F lists $3.06 billion of US stocks across 30 positions.

Since the quarter ended, two of the three have been cut in half or worse.

Microsoft is the steady one

Microsoft was Avala's biggest new position: 400,773 shares worth $206 million at Sept. 30, or 6.7% of its 13F stocks and its third-largest holding. The stock is down 6% since then.

The business hasn't given investors much to worry about. Revenue rose 19% to $92.3 billion in the September quarter, and Azure grew 48%, ahead of the roughly 45% management had guided. Analysts have raised their normalized EPS estimates since late October, to $20.01 for fiscal 2027 and $24.20 for fiscal 2028.

The consensus target has climbed with them, to $636 from a late-July low of $556:

Microsoft (MSFT): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

That's 31% above the last close. And at about 23x forward earnings, Microsoft trades below its 12-year average of 26x and its five-year average of 30x.

TIKR tracks 58 analysts on Microsoft. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Microsoft, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Microsoft's Analyst Ratings

Intel got cheaper, but it isn't cheap

Avala raised its Intel stake 431% in the third quarter, to 1.46 million shares worth $176 million, 5.8% of its 13F stocks. Intel is down 57% since Sept. 30.

Investors sold on the outlook. Intel beat its own guidance in the third quarter, with revenue up 21% to $16.5 billion. But it guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15.0 billion-$16.0 billion and its adjusted gross margin to 38%, down from 44.1%, partly on memory shortages. Then Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO on Nov. 12, and Nvidia's own 13F showed it had cut its Intel stake by about a quarter by Sept. 30.

title: Nvidia Just Issued a Major Warning to AMD and Intel Stock Investors
detail:
Nvidia Just Issued a Major Warning to AMD and Intel Stock Investors
Harsh Chauhan, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 21, 2026 at 6:14 AM CST 5 min read
NVDA
AMD
INTC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) released solid results for the third quarter of fiscal 2027 (which ended on Oct. 25) on Nov. 17 and backed its outstanding performance with impressive guidance.

Its data center business recorded healthy growth once again last quarter, and Nvidia's upgraded guidance for fiscal 2028 suggests that the segment will continue to move the needle substantially next year. However, a closer look at Nvidia's results suggests it is quickly gaining ground in a market where Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) and Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) are the dominant players.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Let's take a closer look at this particular business and check why Nvidia's progress in this space doesn't bode well for Intel and AMD.

Image source: Nvidia.

Nvidia's Vera CPUs are in terrific demand

The market for server central processing units (CPUs) has been growing rapidly amid the increasing adoption of agentic AI and inference applications. This explains why Nvidia decided earlier this year to offer its latest-generation Vera server CPUs as a stand-alone product to customers.

The company already had a server CPU before Vera, known as Grace, but it was available as part of rack-scale systems that integrated graphics cards, networking chips, memory, and other components into a single package. Nvidia's latest quarterly report is proof that its move into the stand-alone server CPU market is paying off.

The product has been adopted by leading hyperscalers, neocloud providers, and AI companies, including Oracle, Meta Platforms, OpenAI, CoreWeave, Nebius, and others. In fact, Nvidia has doubled down on the server CPU market by offering a CPU-based rack-scale server platform to handle agentic AI and inference applications.

Interim CEO Colette Kress remarked on the latest earnings call:

We continue to see very strong demand for Vera and expect total CPU revenue to more than double in fiscal year 2028.

Though the company didn't specify exactly how much revenue it generated from stand-alone sales of the Vera CPU last quarter, it noted on the fiscal Q1 earnings call that it expects $20 billion in revenue from this product in fiscal 2027. Assuming the estimate is still intact, Nvidia's Vera VPU revenue could jump to at least $40 billion next fiscal year.

This should set the alarm bells ringing for AMD and Nvidia investors.

George Soros made his name betting against currencies and central banks, and that record is still the reference point for macro investing decades later. Born in Budapest in 1930, he built his fortune running the Quantum Fund, and the firm that carries his name has been investing for more than five decades.

Soros Fund Management is no longer a hedge fund in the ordinary sense. It returned outside money years ago and now runs as a family office, which means it has no outside investors to report to and can hold a position for as long as it likes. That freedom shows up in the filings.

The firm's latest quarterly disclosure, covering the three months to the end of September and filed in the middle of November, lists 263 separate positions worth about $8.51 billion in total. What stands out is the composition rather than the size. Two of the three largest disclosed positions were put options on energy index funds rather than holdings of shares, and a further $1.17 billion sits in convertible notes. Positions in shares account for a little under two-thirds of the total.

AMD Is Down 26% and Intel Is Down 42%. Which AI Stock Is Worth Buying on the Dip?
RJ Fulton, The Motley Fool

INTC
OPAI.PVT

The recent semiconductor sell-off has presented investors with potentially attractive buying opportunities as concerns surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) valuations weigh on the sector. Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) have fallen approximately 26% and 42% from their respective recent highs.

AMD has established itself as a major supplier of high-performance computing products, capitalizing on growing demand for AI infrastructure. Intel, meanwhile, is pursuing an ambitious turnaround centered on restoring its competitive position in processor design and semiconductor manufacturing.

While both companies stand to benefit from continued investment in AI, their contrasting financial performance, capital requirements, and competitive positions present two distinct investment opportunities.

The case for Advanced Micro Devices

AMD designs high-performance processors and accelerators for data centers, personal computers, and gaming systems. Its expanding portfolio of AI accelerators and multiyear strategic partnership with OpenAI position the company to capture a greater share of AI infrastructure spending. Meanwhile, established relationships with companies such as Sony and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) provide additional revenue streams through its gaming business.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 26, 2026, revenue reached approximately $45.4 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 41.9%. AMD generated $7.6 billion in net income over the same period, translating to a profit margin of roughly 16.8%. Its ability to deliver substantial revenue growth while maintaining profitability is particularly attractive as investors increasingly scrutinize the financial performance of AI-related companies.

As of December 2025, AMD maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.1 and a current ratio of 2.9, reflecting a relatively strong balance sheet. The company also generated approximately $6.7 billion in free cash flow during fiscal 2025, although stock-based compensation accounted for 21.2% of operating cash flow.

The case for Intel

Intel designs and manufactures processors for personal computers, data centers, and networking applications. While its established processor business remains a significant source of revenue, much of Intel's long-term investment thesis centers on its foundry strategy. By expanding its semiconductor manufacturing capabilities, Intel aims to compete for manufacturing contracts from other chip designers while reducing its reliance on traditional processor sales.

An Intel sign out front of a corporate office by wolterke via Adobe Stock

Chip giant Intel (INTC) has had a bumpy 2026, and investors have felt every jolt. The stock hit as high as $142.35 in June, only to give up those gains and fall to around $53. The big hit came after Intel's third-quarter earnings on Oct. 29. The results looked good on paper, but the company warned that fourth-quarter revenue would come in lower than expected, blaming a sluggish PC market and manufacturing bottlenecks. Investors didn't take it well.

On Oct. 30, INTC stock dropped nearly 29%, its biggest one-day fall in decades. The steep drop has since opened another front for the company, with shareholders taking legal action over alleged misleading disclosures. This month, shareholders filed a lawsuit against Intel, claiming CEO Lip-Bu Tan and CFO David Zinsner "engaged in a scheme to deceive the market." The proposed class action, filed in federal court in California by Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd for The City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System, says the two leaders didn't share how big the PC slowdown really was.

Investors argue this "artificially inflated" the stock price and amounted to fraud. Intel is also reportedly cutting jobs again, according to Business Insider. Employees have posted on social media about layoffs in the company's IT team. The company had about 81,000 employees at the end of September, down from roughly 85,000 at the end of 2025. The good news for investors is that layoffs are costing less than before. Intel spent $55 million on severance and benefits last quarter, compared with $146 million in the September 2025 quarter.

So far this year, the company has spent $290 million, versus $1.754 billion in 2025. With operational challenges persisting and investor confidence under pressure, the road ahead looks increasingly uncertain. So, should investors approach INTC stock now?

About Intel Stock

Intel has spent the past few years navigating a difficult stretch, but the semiconductor heavyweight is now undergoing a significant transformation. Founded in 1968 and headquartered in Santa Clara, California, the company built its reputation on the processors that power PCs. However, its ambitions now reach well beyond traditional computing.
